newsitem.title: TURKEY: GWC Turkish markets board defends disclosure rule.
newsitem.headline: GWC Turkish markets board defends disclosure rule.

text.p: Turkey's Capital Markets Board (SPK) on Thursday vowed to maintain a rule requiring brokers to disclose their clients' names, which has raised concerns among foreign institutions active in the Turkish market.
This week the SPK began to enforce the rule following investigations into reported manipulation of shares in Turkish Airlines (THY), an SPK official told Reuters.
The deputy head of the SPK's enforcement department, Cemal Kucuksozen, said the SPK launched an official investigation into Turkish Airlines share manipulation in August.

On August 14 the SPK sent letters to foreign institutions, including Morgan Stanley, SG Warburg, Union Bank of Switzerland and Salomon Brothers, asking for them to disclose the names of their clients.
None of these banks has disclosed names so far, because of which the SPK has been unable to complete its investigations, Kucuksozen said.
"Brokers should give their client's identity, otherwise they will not be able to execute their orders," Kucuksozen told Reuters.
He said the decision to enforce the rule follows a refusal by foreign institutions to disclose clients' identities when requested to do so in the case of THY.
London banks, concerned that the rule could be exploited by local brokers, are in the process of responding to Turkish authorities.
"We are drafting a letter to the Turkish authorities," said Peter Beales, director responsible for compliance at the London Investment Bankers Association.

London banks are expected to protest that the rule as it stands, by discouraging foreign investment, will be damaging to the Turkish market and propose other ways for the markets board to achieve its objective.
The general international approach in the case of an investigation is for one regulator to invite its counterpart abroad to ask firms to cooperate with that investigation.
But Kucuksozen defended the Turkish approach, saying client's names would remain secret and only be consulted in the case of an investigation.
The Istanbul stock exchange settlements bank TAKASBANK said on Thursday that the names of foreign investors would be kept in closed envelopes under lock and key.
One broker who declined to be named said the board was being "heavy-handed" in addressing the issue of manipulation and said constant surveillance of the market was the best safeguard of standards.
He said the concern is that local brokers will be able to obtain client information for their own trading interests.
But Volkan Sari, market strategist at Turkey's leading brokerage Global Securities, said he felt the new regulation was "reasonable."
"I think this is reasonable and I think it is the right thing to do," Sari said, citing the reports of price manipulation.
An extended rally over the last month has lifted the stock market index to consecutive all-time highs. At the close on Wednesday the index had gained 22.7 percent since September 13.
On Thursday the index fell back 3.9 percent midsession to 76,421.09.
